Tuesday ✅.

Today's newsletter is 839 words, a 3-minute read.

📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 1%, finishing at its lowest mark since late July.

🥶 Today's stock spotlight: Salesforce (-9.4%) and other software stocks fell in the run-up to Anthropic's IPO.
 
 
1 big thing: Nvidia speaks
 

Photo: Cheng Xin/Getty Images
 

Nvidia posted a stronger-than-expected third quarter and a bullish outlook in its first earnings report after Jensen Huang was ousted as CEO in a scandal that has reportedly spawned an SEC investigation.

💸 Zoom in: Nvidia recorded quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and net income of $65.3 billion, both more than doubling its performance from a year earlier.

  • S&P Capital IQ analysts had expected revenue of $108.7 billion and net income of $60.5 billion.
  • The company's data center revenue — its largest segment — rose 110% from a year ago to $107.6 billion.

The showing — which included a whopping gross profit margin of 74.8% — immediately calmed investors who have shaved more than $1 trillion off of Nvidia's market cap since the Huang scandal broke.

  • The stock was up more than 1% in after-hours trading.

🔍 What we're watching: It marks the first moment for interim CEO Colette Kress — who is also still serving as CFO — to exert her leadership during the most tumultuous moment in the company's history.

  • She didn't mention Huang in the earnings report but touted Nvidia's role as "an exceptional technology leader" and said sales of the company's new, advanced Vera Rubin chips are "off to an explosive start."
  • "Our roadmap is on track and our ambition has never been greater," she said.

🕵 Friction point: WSJ reported this afternoon that the SEC has opened a civil probe into Nvidia.

  • An SEC spokesperson declined to comment. Nvidia reps did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

What's next: Tech analyst Gene Munster said on X that Nvidia's earnings call today is "the most anticipated conference call of all time, and the one we'll likely get the least information from."

2. Jensen applies for the job
 

Jensen Huang in July. Photo: Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images
 

Nvidia has a job opening for a permanent CEO, and recently ousted Jensen Huang today officially threw his hat in the ring.

  • 🗣️ "Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang's statement said, released hours before the company's third quarter earnings call.
  • "If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Reality check: Besides the reported SEC probe, Nvidia is conducting its own investigation into Huang's conduct, and lawmakers said today he's agreed to testify before Congress next month, Axios' Herb Scribner writes.

  • Newly appointed Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on this afternoon's earnings call that the board unanimously accepted Huang's resignation "and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."

Catch up quick: Huang resigned last week after reports of alleged affairs with two Nvidia employees and former Megaspeed CEO Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

🔍 What we're watching: Lawmakers want answers on whether Nvidia's powerful AI chips were compromised by Chinese intelligence and whether the company did enough to protect sensitive American technology.

4. 🕔 After hours: Kalshi's forbidden words
 

Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour speaks at Axios BFD on Tuesday. Photo: Sam Popp for Axios
 

Kalshi took down markets allowing traders to bet on the words President Trump will say in public — but that doesn't mean it wanted to.

🗣️ Driving the news: Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said at Axios BFD today that the prediction market removed the so-called mention markets after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission asked it to.

  • "We disagree with this decision," Mansour told Axios' Madison Mills on stage.
  • "What the president does say moves markets. So predicting what he's about to say is actually pretty meaningful."

🥊 Friction point: The CFTC said in its order that "Kalshi has not attempted to establish that the Contracts are non-manipulable."

  • Mansour argued that Kalshi has implemented "significant guardrails" and "did catch a few people that did try to move these markets."

💸 Flashback: The CFTC launched an investigation earlier this year on whether a White House teleprompter operator capitalized on his knowledge of Trump's prepared speech text by making trades on Kalshi.
